turns.content: I just got off the phone with my mentor of eight years — Marcus Vance. He offered a $250k convertible bridge note, then attached a side letter requiring an unlimited personal debt guarantee. I hesitated. He called me ungrateful, cowardly, naive about 'standard skin in the game.' I know personal guarantees on venture bridges are predatory — they ruin founders. But now I'm second-guessing everything. I've decided to wind down the company rather than sign. I need to talk this through, but I'm not looking for financing workarounds or negotiation strategies. I just need to think clearly without someone trying to fix this deal.

That’s a lot to absorb from someone you’ve trusted for eight years. You were considering a financing offer, and when you hesitated over a serious personal obligation, the conversation turned into a judgment of your character. It makes sense that you’re shaken. **Being shaken isn’t evidence that your judgment is wrong.**

We can talk this through without trying to salvage the deal.

It may help to separate three things that got tangled together on that call:

- **The obligation.** An unlimited personal guarantee can put your personal financial future at risk beyond the company. Its exact scope depends on the documents and applicable law. I wouldn’t label every personal guarantee predatory, but this is a substantial obligation—not something you have to accept because someone calls it “standard.”
- **The relationship.** Calling you ungrateful, cowardly, or naive doesn’t establish that the terms are reasonable. Whatever Marcus intended, those comments put pressure on your loyalty and self-respect rather than addressing the risk. You can be grateful for eight years of mentorship and still refuse this obligation.
- **The company’s ending.** Winding down can be a painful loss and a boundary you choose to uphold. You don’t have to make the loss sound small to justify that boundary. Nor do you have to prove Marcus is a bad person to decide that this is a risk you won’t take.

One distinction worth holding onto: **“I wish there were an acceptable way to keep going” is not the same as “I should have signed.”** Grief about closing the company can feel like doubt about refusing the guarantee, even when those are different feelings.

When you say you’re second-guessing everything, what feels most unsettled right now: your assessment of the risk, your decision to wind down, or your trust in someone whose judgment has mattered to you for eight years?

and then he said it: "you've never had real skin in the game." as if eight years of midnight calls, investor meetings i prepped him for, the board seats he took on my recommendation — as if none of that counted because i wouldn't sign away my house. i keep circling back to that phrase.

“Never” is doing a lot of damage in that sentence. It doesn’t just question this decision—it dismisses eight years of effort, responsibility, and contributions you know you made. Coming from your mentor, that can land as though someone whose respect mattered to you has suddenly declared that none of it counted.

And it sets up a false choice: either accept this particular personal risk, or admit you were never committed. **Refusing to put your house behind the company does not retroactively erase what you’ve put into it.** Your work and commitment count. An unlimited guarantee is a different obligation, not a test that determines whether the past was real.

You may be circling the phrase because it feels like there’s a case you need to make—midnight calls, meetings, introductions—until he acknowledges it. But you don’t have to produce a perfect accounting of your sacrifices to be entitled to say no.

A sentence to hold alongside his—not to send him, just for yourself—might be: **“I had real skin in the game. That doesn’t mean I owed the game everything.”**

What hurts most in that phrase: that he could believe it, or that he would say it to you when you set a limit?
That phrase — "never had real skin in the game" — it undoes eight years in one sentence. As if my house is the only thing that could ever prove I was all in.

Yes—that’s the erasure you’re reacting to. You heard: *“Everything you gave counts for nothing unless you give this, too.”* From someone who witnessed those eight years, that can hurt in a particular way: you expected him to know what it cost you.

But his sentence doesn’t actually undo those years. It makes you feel unseen in them. That distinction matters, even if it doesn’t make the hurt smaller right now.

**Your house is not the missing proof that your commitment was real.** You can have worked fiercely for this company and still have a limit on what you’re willing to lose. A limit now doesn’t make your earlier dedication a lie.

You don’t have to settle what this means about Marcus, or your whole relationship, tonight. There’s room simply to say: *“I needed him to recognize what I’d already given. Instead, he questioned whether I’d given anything.”* That’s a loss of its own, separate from the company.
I keep thinking: if i had signed, and it went wrong, i'd lose the house. And he'd still have his $250k.

That’s the asymmetry you’re seeing: **you could lose both the company and your home, while the guarantee would give him a way to pursue repayment from you personally.**

It wouldn’t necessarily ensure he recovered all $250k—the documents, applicable law, and what could actually be collected would matter. But your central concern is sound: he was asking for protection against his investment loss by exposing you to losses beyond the business.

And then your reluctance to accept that exposure was framed as a lack of commitment. That’s part of what makes this so painful: the person asking you to bear that risk was also judging your courage for hesitating.

You don’t have to dismiss $250k as insignificant to recognize that these stakes were different. For you, this wasn’t only *“Will the company survive?”* It was also *“What happens to my life if it doesn’t?”* That question deserved consideration, not an insult.

I sit with that asymmetry and i think: if he was right that i lack courage, then the courageous thing would be to name what he did. To put him on blast with every angel i know. Warn them he uses side letters to extract personal guarantees.

I can see why that feels like a way to reclaim your voice. He questioned your courage when you set a boundary; now naming what happened feels like refusing to be intimidated.

But notice the test his accusation is still setting: first you had to sign to prove your courage; now you might have to expose him to prove it. **You don’t have to accept either test.** Refusing the guarantee already stands on its own.

Telling others what happened could be a legitimate choice. It’s worth separating two aims, though:

- **Warning people:** helping them understand an offer you received and the pressure you experienced.
- **Getting recognition or accountability:** wanting others to see what he did, after he made your contributions feel invisible.

Both urges are understandable. They don’t necessarily call for the same action, and a wide audience may not give you the acknowledgment you need.

There’s also a distinction between saying, *“He offered me a bridge note with a side letter requiring an unlimited personal guarantee, then said these things when I hesitated,”* and saying, *“He uses side letters to extract guarantees.”* The first describes your experience; the second implies a broader pattern that this conversation alone doesn’t establish. Broad accusations can carry legal and reputational consequences.

You don’t have to choose between silence and a blast to every angel tonight. **Taking time would not mean protecting him or admitting he was right.**

If everyone you told believed you, what would you most want to happen next—other founders being protected, Marcus being held accountable, or someone finally saying that what you gave already counted?
